claims.text: Adding a finely dispersed, thermally stable oxide phase such as Y2O3 to the HEA will increase yield strength.
Adding oxide dispersoids will increase resistance to radiation-induced degradation.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will preserve phase stability at high temperature.
The proposed baseline is a single-phase, near-equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi-type HEA.
Inherent lattice distortion gives the baseline HEA some irradiation tolerance.
Powder metallurgy or an in situ dispersion technique can produce a controlled few-volume-percent oxide dispersion in the HEA.
The intervention will produce nanoscale, uniformly dispersed oxide particles within the HEA matrix.
Oxide dispersoids will pin dislocations and impede their motion during deformation.
Oxide dispersoids will act as sinks or traps for irradiation-induced point defects and helium atoms.
Trapping defects and helium at oxide dispersoids will limit helium-bubble growth and coalescence.
Suppressing large helium bubbles should mitigate irradiation hardening because large, dense bubbles interact with dislocations and increase hardness.
Sequential Kr and He irradiation can cause helium accumulation, large stress changes, and increased dislocation density in CoCrFeMnNi.
Sequential heavy- and light-ion irradiation simulates fission-product and transmutation conditions.
The predicted benefits will persist during service above 0.5 times the melting temperature.
Relative to an undoped HEA under identical exposure, the oxide-dispersed HEA will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the undoped baseline, the oxide-dispersed HEA will exhibit less irradiation-induced hardening and less defect coalescence or phase instability.
The beneficial effects require oxide particles to be appropriately sized and well dispersed.
Excessive oxide content may cause embrittlement or undesirable secondary phases, whereas insufficient dispersion may produce no appreciable effect.
